claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a standard near-surface microstructure and oxide state.
Corrosion protection of pre-exposure Q235 steel is mainly governed by the integrity of an in situ formed oxide layer.
At room temperature, controlled oxidation of Q235 steel forms a coherent, dense oxide scale.
The room-temperature oxide scale impedes further corrosive attack on Q235 steel.
Oxidation of Q235 steel becomes rapid at 700–900 °C under aggressive salt exposure.
Salt-induced fluxing at 700–900 °C causes the oxide scale on Q235 steel to become porous and defective.
A porous or defective oxide scale loses barrier effectiveness and accelerates corrosion.
Pre-annealing modifies the near-surface microstructure and oxide-nucleation behavior of Q235 steel.
Pre-annealing may refine grain size or reduce defect density in Q235 steel.
Pre-annealing may promote a more stable oxide on Q235 steel at elevated temperature.
As-received Q235 steel will corrode relatively slowly at room temperature because of protective oxide formation.
As-received Q235 steel will undergo accelerated corrosion with oxide-scale porosity or spallation at 700–900 °C under salt exposure.
Pre-annealed Q235 steel will develop a denser, less porous oxide scale than untreated Q235 steel at high temperature.
Pre-annealed Q235 steel will have a lower high-temperature corrosion rate than untreated Q235 steel.
A corrosion-resistant stainless-based reference consistently forms stable oxide scales at both room temperature and 700–900 °C.
The proposed mechanism applies when corrosion is dominated by salt-driven changes in oxide-scale integrity.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply when alloying or protective treatments fundamentally alter oxidation kinetics or when corrosion is not controlled by oxide-scale integrity.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says pre-annealing only may improve oxide stability and the uncertainty field acknowledges that its influence is unknown, but the prediction treats improvement as expected and the falsification rule treats failure of that optional effect as falsifying the broader oxide-integrity mechanism.
